name: William Chambers Monument
description: This statue honours Sir William Chambers (1800-1883), the publisher-turned-Lord-Provost who reshaped this part of the Old Town more than almost anyone else. He and his brother Robert built a printing and publishing empire from a small Peebles bookshop, but it was as Lord Provost from 1865 that Chambers left his biggest mark: pushing through the 1867 Edinburgh Improvement Act, which cleared entire slum closes and cut new streets - including the one that now bears his name - through some of the city's most overcrowded ground. Sculpted by John Rhind on a plinth by H.J. Blanc, the statue was erected in 1891, originally standing in the middle of Chambers Street itself.
interesting_fact: The statue was moved to its current position in 2016, when the pedestrian area was widened to make room for a second, similarly styled statue directly nearby - William Henry Playfair, the architect whose buildings Chambers Street was built to celebrate.
source_notes: History from Canmore/trove.scot and edinburghexpert.com. Google Places confirms Chambers Street location. Leg assigned by geography (nearest existing leg-11 POI, Greyfriars Bobby Statue).

name: William Henry Playfair Monument
description: Standing a few steps from the William Chambers monument it deliberately echoes, this statue honours William Henry Playfair (1790-1857), the architect behind more of Edinburgh's best-known buildings than perhaps any other single figure - the National Gallery, the Royal Scottish Academy, the National Monument on Calton Hill and Surgeons' Hall among them. Sculpted by Alexander Stoddart and unveiled in 2016, it deliberately mirrors the style, scale and pose of the older Chambers statue nearby, portraying Playfair in period dress with papers in hand, as though caught mid-design.
interesting_fact: The statue was commissioned specifically to give Playfair - whose neoclassical buildings define huge parts of central Edinburgh's skyline - the same kind of permanent public recognition long since given to Chambers, more than 125 years after the earlier statue went up a few metres away.
source_notes: History from Edinburgh World Heritage (ewh.org.uk) and Scotsman coverage of the 2016 unveiling. Google Places confirms Chambers Street location, ~90m from the Chambers monument. Checked for duplicate - no prior 'Playfair' statue POI exists; distinct from any building he designed.

name: Hotel du Vin & Bistro
description: This boutique hotel occupies a cluster of former institutional buildings dating back to 1743, which over the centuries served in turn as a poorhouse, an asylum, and later a science laboratory, before Hotel du Vin restored and connected them into a single luxury hotel. Ten of its rooms sit within the original historic buildings, kept deliberately atmospheric, while a newer wing built onto the site matches them in style. The hotel keeps a whisky snug and a specialist wine-tasting room among its features, alongside its bistro and mezzanine bar, trading on the contrast between the building's institutional past and its now thoroughly comfortable present.
interesting_fact: Guests booking the hotel's older rooms are, in effect, staying inside a converted 18th-century asylum - one of several former asylums and poorhouses across Edinburgh's Old Town that have been repurposed for hospitality rather than demolished.
source_notes: Building history (1743, poorhouse/asylum/science lab) from edinburgh-hotel.org and Michelin Guide. Google Places confirms 11 Bristo Place. Leg assigned by geography (46m from Bedlam Theatre, existing leg-11 POI).
